arxiv:2611.03178.text: CoworkOS:Scaling Agent Coworkers for Real-world Automation. From Jiajie Jin and colleagues. Long-running productivity tasks require agents to deliver complex work while staying coordinated with people over time. CoworkOS is a system that separates planning from execution and lets agents delegate tasks, share evolving files with people, and preserve work and decisions across sessions. Across twelve benchmarks and six application areas, it performed competitively with leading agent tools. In a five-round post-training study, it also raised a model's average score across eight benchmarks from 33.19 to 42.95.

arxiv:2611.00859.text: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation. From Yijie Jin and colleagues. Streaming long videos quickly is difficult because existing chunk-by-chunk methods can be inefficient and may lose visual consistency or drift over time. Wave Forcing combines a training method with a generation system that overlaps denoising and cache updates, producing one video chunk per forward round after startup. In tests, five-step generation matched Rolling Forcing's overall quality and achieved higher motion levels on short and long videos. On eight H200 graphics cards, four-step generation reached 134.8 end-to-end frames per second.

arxiv:2611.03126.text: CUA-Master: Scaling Computer-use Agents through Open-World Recursive Improvements. From Xinlei Yu and colleagues. Computer-use agents are held back by interaction data that is too limited, and by training methods that do not learn from repeated feedback. CUA-Master builds a two-level improvement loop: it turns instructional videos into realistic tasks, then reuses task elements to create varied, complex examples that can be checked. It also uses feedback to retry failed interactions in real environments. Its twenty-seven-billion-parameter model performs competitively across computer-use benchmarks, while repeated improvement continues to raise performance.

arxiv:2611.01560.text: Democratizing Robot-Use Agents: A Unified Harness with Open Models. From Jiarui Yuan and colleagues. Robot-use agents can manipulate objects without task-specific training, but reliance on proprietary models makes it harder to study how to improve them. This work introduces an open harness that supports competitive robot use and further training, without giving models privileged inputs. Using it, an open Qwen model scores 31.39 on RoboDojo, above the published score of 28.97 for a proprietary model, and performs competitively on nineteen real-world tasks. The analysis points to four general capabilities that future training should develop together.

arxiv:2611.02102.text: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale. From Chaoyun Zhang and colleagues. Computer-use agents need experience that links individual actions to complete software tasks. NorthCUA creates executable tasks, records long interactions, checks outcomes, and turns successful attempts into reusable training examples and skills. It then trains and improves agents through staged learning and fresh desktop and web attempts. Its Nano, Mini, and Pro models achieve state-of-the-art results among open-source models on the reported tests, while a faster version trades some quality for lower response time.

arxiv:2611.02897.text: PhotoGuider: Composition-Aware Cropping and 360to the View Framing with Explainable Photographic Assessments. From Yuan-Kang Lee and colleagues. Cropping tools usually assume the best part of a photo is already in view. But with a full 360-degree scene, they must first find the right viewing direction, then frame it. PhotoGuider measures subjects, composition, aesthetics, and image integrity, then uses those assessments to choose a direction and produce a crop, with explanations and camera settings for re-rendering. It achieved the highest average overlap with reference crops on two standard benchmarks, and viewers ranked its panoramic framings first in 53.2 percent of cases.

arxiv:2611.00172.text: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings. From Ziyin Zhang and colleagues. Embedding research is split into separate communities for different kinds of data, even though many models share underlying ideas. This survey traces how contrastive learning, Transformer designs, and finer-grained representations are bringing the field closer together, while highlighting challenges that remain specific to each modality. It organizes progress around coverage, comparability, and compositionality, and argues that transformation, alignment, and ultimately joint embedding offer a roadmap toward unified omnimodal systems.

arxiv:2611.01815.text: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models? From Anton Hristov and colleagues. Video world models can make prediction errors for reasons other than surprising physics, including changes in appearance or ordinary difficulty. This study compares frozen video representations and tests how their prediction errors respond to different changes. V-JEPA2 contains modest information about whether events are physically possible, but appearance changes also affect errors, and impossible events can even produce lower errors than possible ones. So a model may represent physical information without its own error reliably measuring physical surprise.

arxiv:2611.01860.text: Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics. From Hengyu Liu and colleagues. Research on artificial intelligence agents that write and refine graphics code is growing quickly, but inconsistent terms make it hard to track and compare. This report introduces a shared framework for describing these systems and a tool that helps researchers analyze both existing and newly published work at scale. It uses these contributions to map emerging trends and highlight challenges in coordinating agents and tools, supporting human collaboration, handling long tasks, and evaluating interactive graphics systems.

arxiv:2611.03344.text: FLAMIA: FLAsh MIcroscaling Attention for Fast and Causally Safe Training on Blackwell. From Fedor Velikonivtsev and colleagues. Long-context attention is a major cost in Transformer training, and low-precision hardware can introduce causal leakage and mismatched computations during training. FLAMIA is a set of attention kernels for Blackwell graphics processors that combines low-precision formats with safeguards for causal masking, consistent forward and backward passes, and support for packed documents. Across tested workloads, its MXFP8 version made the full attention call, including quantization, up to one point four times faster than the fastest baseline. Pretraining tests also showed stable training and preserved quality.

arxiv:2611.03602.text: Reviso: Not All Visual Evidence Deserves Equal Attention in Video Captioning. From Tengfei Liu and colleagues. Video captioning systems can fixate on small details and miss the context or events that matter most. Reviso first scans a video, then plans what to inspect and revisits selected moments with tools for closer analysis. It is trained to favor accurate key facts, useful observation targets, and efficient tool use. Across four captioning benchmarks, Reviso outperforms the tested open-source systems, and its captions better support answering questions about videos.

arxiv:2611.03092.text: Avatar Intelligence: Amplifying Human Agency Through Persistent Personal Agents. From Zheng Wu and colleagues. Personal artificial intelligence agents can handle extended tasks, but people still spend time explaining goals, clearing up uncertainty, and checking results. Avatar Intelligence proposes persistent agents that carry a person's goals, values, and limits across tasks, while leaving important decisions under human control. It outlines stages from human-led work to autonomy within agreed domains, and a way to weigh benefits against operating costs and oversight. The agenda highlights lasting personalization, learning through rehearsal, and safety with accountability and recourse.

arxiv:2611.03526.text: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime. From Abdellah Rahmani and colleagues. Language models usually run their layers in a fixed order, limiting how they can adapt their computation to different tasks. Library of Layers lets a model choose the order of transformer blocks at runtime, using one setting to balance shared parameters against sparse computation. On text, it performs competitively with dense, recurrent, and mixture-of-experts models. On puzzles, its layer orderings reflect different solution strategies, and researchers can steer those strategies; its routing also varies across languages and can distinguish safe from unsafe text.

arxiv:2611.01484.text: CrossSWE: Benchmarking Cross-Repository Joint Development for Coding Agents. From Silin Chen and colleagues. Software engineering benchmarks often test changes within one repository, but real development can require coordinated work across several connected repositories. CrossSWE introduces a benchmark of 171 real-world tasks, covering 165 repositories, and checks that changing only part of a project is not enough. In tests of five language models, the strongest passed 58.48 percent of tasks on its first attempt. The most common failure was inconsistency between repositories.

arxiv:2611.02633.text: Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence. From Sean Wu and colleagues. As artificial intelligence agents increasingly work with people and other agents, solo performance does not show whether they make good teammates. The Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark tests teamwork across 240 tasks drawn from real records and existing benchmarks, scoring models only on tasks they can solve alone with full information. Across 18 models, even the top score was 82.2 out of 100, and models with similar general ability differed as teammates. Strong models often resisted unsafe shortcuts but struggled under interpersonal pressure and when checking work left by a weaker model.

arxiv:2611.02074.text: SWE-Trail: History-Guided Trajectory Collection for Coding Agent Training. From Ziming Li and colleagues. Coding agents learn from their problem-solving traces, but collecting many traces independently can produce increasingly repetitive examples. SWE-Trail uses earlier traces to decide where more collection may be useful, while keeping that history hidden from the coding agent. At those points, the agent proposes possible next steps, and the system briefly tests them to choose a route. Models trained on these traces resolved more issues than models trained on independently sampled traces, with gains of two point three three percentage points on SWE-bench Multilingual and one point six on SWE-bench Pro.

arxiv:2611.02332.text: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents. From Sreehari Sankar and colleagues. Tool-using language models can make calls that violate the rules of their environment. LeanGuard checks each proposed call against policies written in Lean, including rules about past actions, and blocks calls that fail the check. On Tau-Bench, unguarded agents made at least thirty-three forbidden calls, while LeanGuard made none; feedback did not significantly change task success. On DTap, it cut direct prompt-injection success from fifty-seven point nine percent to five point nine percent.

arxiv:2611.02928.text: Lab2Sim: Turning Real-World Experiment Videos into Interactive Virtual Experiments. From Xusen Hei and colleagues. Science experiment videos show what to do, but learners cannot interact with them, and turning them into virtual experiments means capturing both the equipment and the rules for each step. Lab2Sim benchmarks this challenge with 218 videos and nearly twelve thousand scoring items, while EduVideo2Code turns procedures into step-by-step state machines and checks the generated pages by running them. Existing models can make pages that run but often get the equipment wrong; EduVideo2Code improves all four evaluation measures, including apparatus fidelity by 24.15 points.

arxiv:2611.03393.text: TaoMate-FVSR:Audio-Guided Facial Video Restoration. From Xinyang Li and colleagues. AI-generated videos can show detailed scenes but leave faces too blurry to tell whether the lips and teeth match the speech. TaoMate-FVSR restores facial video using both audio and visual references, starting from partly preserved observations and separating stable appearance from changing motion. Training also teaches it to correct dubbed footage when the audio changes. On talking-head benchmarks, it achieved the strongest combination of perceptual similarity and audio-video synchronization among the compared restoration methods.

arxiv:2611.01460.text: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos? From Haoyu Zhao and colleagues. Language model agents often cannot carry lessons from tutorial videos into later tasks, and updating their parameters is costly. Tutorial Agentic Learning builds a persistent, structured memory from videos, refining it with challenging questions grounded in their content. On a new benchmark of chess tutorials, it beat all tested alternatives, improved as it processed more videos, and reached stronger opening positions in most head-to-head games. Tests in another domain also suggest the approach can extend beyond chess.

arxiv:2611.03558.text: Quantum Private Information Retrieval on Forests. From Mohamed Nomeir and colleagues. Quantum private information retrieval lets a user retrieve data without revealing which item they want, but its performance on forest graphs has been unclear. For forests, which are collections of disjoint trees, the work designs a scheme where servers share an entangled Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state and each sends one qudit per round. The scheme reaches a rate of three over the number of servers and is more efficient than the earlier quantum graph retrieval scheme. For the graph made of three separate edges, it also proves the best possible rate is four sixths.

arxiv:2611.02122.text: Optimal spectral shrinkage via Krylov approximation. From Tianfeng Lu and colleagues. Spectral shrinkage can improve prediction in large regression problems, but its best filter depends on unknown features of the data. Risk-targeted Krylov fitting chooses a filter from a compact set of directions by directly minimizing leave-one-out prediction error, without refitting the model for each data point. The method reaches the best risk available in that set up to an error that shrinks with sample size, and approaches the best analytic filter with a number of directions that grows only logarithmically. In tests, it was robust to that choice and usually predicted better than competing methods on biological data.

arxiv:2611.03475.text: Structured Neural Network Models for Anisotropic Magnetic Constitutive Laws. From Dorian Zeilinger and colleagues. Modeling electrical steel is difficult because its magnetic response is nonlinear and varies with direction, which can complicate field simulations. This work uses a structured neural network to describe the steel's anisotropic, anhysteretic response. It builds a smooth, convex co-energy density with controlled behavior at large field strengths, supporting physical consistency and reliable numerical methods. Numerical tests show that the model captures strong anisotropy and converges robustly in finite-element simulations.

arxiv:2611.03442.text: Subpolynomial-Query Proximal Sampling Beyond Log-Concavity. From Wei Guo and colleagues. Sampling from complex distributions is difficult when their energy function is not convex, even if its gradient changes smoothly. This work builds a proximal sampling method that alternates Gaussian noise with sampling a position given the noisy observation, using a high-order conditional sampler to reduce the number of gradient queries. Under a log-Sobolev inequality, it achieves a query count that grows only as a fixed, arbitrarily small power of the problem parameters. Under a Poincaré inequality, it gives a guarantee from a suitably warm start, and shows that a stationary point alone is not enough.

arxiv:2611.03596.text: Spacetime Emergence in the Memory of a Learning Agent. From Philip A. LeMaitre and colleagues. The work asks whether an agent can recover spacetime's causal structure without being told the geometry. A model-based reinforcement-learning agent learns to maximize quantum mutual information between localized probes interacting with a quantum field in Minkowski spacetime. Its internal predictive model develops the characteristic lightlike structure of spacetime, and the causal structure of the Minkowski metric can then be reconstructed with high accuracy. This suggests that spacetime concepts can emerge from an agent's quantum experience and actions.

arxiv:2611.03610.text: A GPU Engine for Sparse Matrix-Vector Products on k squared-Tree-Compressed Graphs. From Francesco Tosoni and colleagues. Large graphs can exceed GPU memory when stored in conventional sparse formats, while compressed graph traversal can leave the GPU waiting on memory. This work builds a GPU engine for multiplying vectors by graphs stored as compact k-squared trees, using parallel tree traversal and bounded temporary storage. It supports products in either direction, batches of vectors, and several common kinds of arithmetic. Across fourteen graphs, the trees were two point three to twenty-seven times smaller than cuSPARSE storage; the engine is especially useful when memory, rather than speed, is the main constraint.

arxiv:2611.03466.text: A Bayesian Framework for Safe Optimal Control of Unknown Systems from Input-Output Data. From Robert Lefringhausen and colleagues. Safe control of an unknown system is difficult when its dynamics are nonlinear or random, its internal state cannot be measured, and data are scarce. This work combines these challenges in a Bayesian framework, using input and output data to estimate both the system dynamics and hidden states. It then provides probabilistic checks for whether constraints will be met and designs a controller that balances performance against risk. Tests on a vertical farm demonstrate the approach, which can update its estimates as new measurements arrive.

arxiv:2611.03440.text: Beyond GNSS: Leveraging LEO Satellite Signals of Opportunity for Doppler Positioning. From Md. Ali Hasan and colleagues. Positioning can fail when global navigation satellite systems are unavailable, and low Earth orbit satellites do not usually send dedicated navigation signals. This work explores how existing satellite signals can be reused, with Doppler shifts and public orbit data helping estimate a user's location. It also introduces a ray tracing tool for realistic, repeatable testing. Simulations show high positioning accuracy in both urban and open-sky settings, supporting this approach as a promising option for future positioning systems.

arxiv:2611.03647.text: Pixel-UMI: Learning Environment-Aware Whole-Body Manipulation from Sensorized Human Demonstrations. From Jason Jingzhou Liu and colleagues. Pixel-UMI tackles the gap between human demonstrations and the way a mobile robot moves and sees its surroundings. It uses scene geometry and human head and hand movements to plan robot poses, then masks views that may not match because of body differences. Human corrections help the robot learn contact-rich actions that demonstrations alone miss. Across five challenging tasks, the approach achieved an average task progress of eighty-seven percent.

arxiv:2611.01857.text: Inference for conditional Fréchet means via Riemannian Robust Bias Correction. From Ryunosuke Miyazaki and colleagues. Estimating conditional averages becomes harder when predictors and outcomes lie on curved spaces, where smoothing can introduce bias that affects confidence statements. This work develops a method that estimates the leading bias in the outcome's tangent space, then corrects the estimate on the manifold. It also accounts for uncertainty in that correction when building confidence sets and bands. The method gives valid pointwise and simultaneous inference without undersmoothing, and simulations show better coverage when smoothing bias matters.

arxiv:2611.03372.text: First- and second-order constrained optimisation for inverse homogenisation of unidirectionally varying microstructure. From Constantin Christof and colleagues. Recovering a material's microscopic structure from large-scale measurements is difficult when that structure varies in one direction. This work proves that the resulting optimisation problem is well posed and derives conditions for its solutions, then analyses two methods for finding them. The methods apply across several kinds of elliptic equations and have guarantees of global convergence. In numerical tests, a new semismooth Newton method needed far fewer costly projection evaluations than gradient descent, making it significantly faster.

arxiv:2611.02956.text: Specification-Aware Predictive Uncertainty Decomposition. From Roman Vashurin and colleagues. Predictive uncertainty usually assumes the input is complete, so it can miss how much an unclear request might change the answer. This work separates prediction risk into uncertainty from missing intent, uncertainty that remains even when intent is known, and uncertainty about the model. It also develops ways to estimate these parts and relates them to existing measures. Across several domains and input types, missing-intent uncertainty best identifies underspecified inputs, while the remaining randomness best flags errors on familiar inputs.

arxiv:2611.02963.text: Full-Rank Constructions of Explicit Lossless Expanders and Good Small-Set qLTCs. From Yali Aharon-Holzman and colleagues. Building quantum low-density parity-check codes with strong error protection has been difficult, especially while keeping their check matrices full rank. This work constructs explicit lossless expanders with full-rank adjacency matrices, then combines pairs of them to build quantum codes with strong protection against errors on small sets. The resulting code family enables, under earlier work's assumptions, quantum memories with an exponentially long guaranteed lifetime at sufficiently low fixed positive temperature, improving on a stretched-exponential guarantee.

arxiv:2611.02808.text: Sketching in Regression: Sketchy in Practice? From Somarddha Das and colleagues. High-dimensional regression can be sped up by compressing the data while preserving the information needed for accurate solutions. This study gives concrete analyses of several such compression methods, including Fast Johnson-Lindenstrauss and OSNAP transforms, and derives lower bounds on how small the compressed dimension can be. The results suggest that, for practical accuracy or computational savings, existing guarantees often require dimensions and data sizes larger than those typically found in practice.

arxiv:2611.03518.text: VIAS: Value-Isolating Activation Steering for Multi-Value Alignment and Compliance for Organisations. From Avni Mittal and colleagues. Large language model agents may need to follow several organisational values at once, but steering methods can blur those values into a general signal for compliance. Value-Isolating Activation Steering builds separate steering vectors by changing whether one value appears in a prompt, while checking that responses still meet the other values. Tested on workplace scenarios, it made the vectors less overlapping, though it did not give independent control over each value. Combined with prompting, it improved compliance across all tagged values for each of three models.

arxiv:2611.03240.text: Susceptibility optimization for wisdom of crowds: A social power reformulation and realization framework. From Ye Tian and colleagues. Crowd estimates can become more biased when some people are more willing than others to change their minds. This work finds how to set that willingness in a model of social influence, by first choosing how much each person's initial estimate should count, then finding the levels of influence that produce those weights. It gives conditions for when the desired weights can be achieved and an algorithm that finds the best solution globally. A distributed version also lets people compute the solution through local communication.

arxiv:2611.03378.text: Non-Coherent Over-the-Air Distributed Consensus: Algorithm Design and Power Control Optimization. From Yuhang Deng and colleagues. Wireless networks can combine local values without precise channel information, but errors in these transmissions can prevent agents from reaching the exact average. This work develops a consensus method that handles row-stochastic mixing, which does not need to preserve averages on its own. The method is shown to converge in mean square to the exact average of the agents' starting values. A power-control scheme that balances transmission accuracy and network mixing significantly speeds convergence compared with full-power transmission and other benchmark methods.

arxiv:2611.03648.text: Pixel: A Co-Designed Full-Stack Robot System for Learning General-Purpose Mobile Manipulation. From Tony Tao and colleagues. Building mobile robots that can handle varied tasks is difficult because hardware, data collection, control, and learning are often designed separately. Pixel brings these pieces together in a low-cost wheeled humanoid, with several ways to collect demonstrations and a shared controller and learning pipeline. Its hierarchical learning system supports language-guided actions and longer tasks. Tests demonstrate behaviors that combine dexterity, perception, navigation, and coordinated movement of the whole robot.

arxiv:2611.01436.text: Transport for Conditional Sampling: Foundations and Applications. From Ricardo Baptista and colleagues. Sampling from a probability model after observing data is important in Bayesian and causal inference, but can be hard when normalizing constants are intractable or each observation demands a new inference task. This article explains how triangular transport maps can turn a reference distribution directly into the desired conditional distribution for any observation. It reviews the theory and algorithms, including ways to estimate these maps from finite samples, and explores applications in simulation-based and causal inference. It also presents new ideas and open questions for the field.

arxiv:2611.03181.text: Multi-GPU Acceleration of Interface Problems in FEniCS, with Application to Cardiac Modeling. From Edoardo Centofanti and colleagues. Mixed-dimensional finite element problems link three-dimensional regions through lower-dimensional interfaces, but automated GPU frameworks have not supported them. This work extends cuDOLFINx to assemble these problems on GPUs, while keeping the familiar FEniCS programming model, and runs the full cardiac EMI model on the GPU. Tests on regular and realistic heart geometries show that one GH200 node assembles about as fast as two 144-core CPU nodes. For solving the equations, GPU performance depends on the geometry and setup, but is faster at every tested scale on the realistic geometry.
